messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Diplomat
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs, Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Vignette:
Aarav, a 24-year-old South Asian man working as a diplomat, came to treatment after months of trying to keep himself composed in a city that, on paper, was now safe but still felt to him as if it could turn violent without warning. His difficulty began during an overseas posting in a war zone, when an ordinary evening meeting at a residence was shattered by the sudden bang of an explosion nearby. In the confusion that followed, he became acutely aware of the smell of alcohol on someone’s breath as people tried to move through the aftermath, a detail that stayed with him with unusual force. He remembers the event in a highly detailed way: the sound, the pressure in the air, the faces around him, the sense that everything had become unreal yet intensely sharp at the same time. When he tries to describe what happened, he often says he knows exactly what occurred but cannot find the words to lay it out in a sequence that makes sense to another person. He can describe fragments, but the memory sits in him more as a vivid set of images, smells, and bodily impressions than as a story he can tell from beginning to end.

In the months after that event, Aarav noticed that certain moments seemed to pull him back into that same state. A loud explosion or even a sudden bang in daily life could make him freeze and feel as though he were right back there. At times, especially when he was already feeling emotionally vulnerable, he found himself suddenly acting as if the danger were happening again, scanning the area and feeling the same immediate alarm that had taken over during the original incident. He became wary of strangers approaching him in ordinary situations, even when others around him appeared calm. On the street, in a café, or in the lobby of his office building, a person walking toward him could be enough to make him feel threatened before anything had actually happened. Even when colleagues or friends reassured him that he was safe, he found it impossible to believe them fully; their confidence did not match his own sense that danger could return without notice.

As time passed, Aarav’s beliefs about people and the world became more guarded. He had come to feel that he had lost faith in people, in life, and in any larger sense of protection he once assumed would be there. He also found himself wondering whether something about him had made the event happen, a private and painful thought that he could not dislodge. Alongside that, he carried a bleak sense that he had no future. These thoughts were not abstract for him; they appeared in quiet moments after work, when he was alone and less able to keep his mind occupied. Although he remained outwardly functional, he increasingly organized his life around not being noticed. He wore concealing clothing when possible, choosing layers and darker, less conspicuous pieces, and he paid close attention to how visible he was in public spaces. In his role as a diplomat, where formal appearance and social contact are part of the job, this habit affected how he moved through receptions, meetings, and the building where he worked. He was careful to stay near exits or to position himself so he would not attract attention, and this vigilance made the ordinary business of greeting people feel exhausting.

Aarav also began using drugs and pushing himself to exercise excessively, both of which became part of the way he tried to get through the day. Exercise gave him a structured way to keep moving, and he often drove himself far beyond what felt moderate, as though rest would leave too much room for the memories and the sense of threat to intrude. Drugs became another way of shutting things down temporarily, though he did not speak about either habit with pride. They were presented as efforts to get relief, not as solutions. Despite these efforts, he remained unsettled, and the contrast between his outward competence and his internal fear became increasingly hard to manage, especially in a job that required him to interact with strangers and remain composed.

He eventually sought help because the combination of being unable to trust that he was safe, being startled back into the experience of the event by bang sounds, and feeling increasingly isolated by his own thoughts had become too difficult to carry alone. He was most afraid that the world would again prove as dangerous as it had been in the war zone, and that he would never be able to feel secure in people or in his own future. At the same time, he hoped for some way to regain a life in which he could move through his work, his relationship, and ordinary public places without feeling as though disaster were always about to break open again.
